title: Architecture and Separation of Concerns
learning_outcomes: Explain the central rule or purpose of architecture and separation of concerns using at least one correct term from the lesson.
Interpret or adapt a small Kotlin example that demonstrates architecture and separation of concerns.
Identify one relevant edge case, debugging step, or version/platform constraint.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn **Architecture and Separation of Concerns** as part of **Software Engineering, Security, and Performance**. Apply architecture and separation of concerns by identifying the required behavior, the relevant Kotlin type/API, and the conditions under which the expected result can fail. Use the subtopics—Layered Architecture, Domain, Application, and Infrastructure Responsibilities, Module Boundaries—as a checklist: predict what the example will do, then verify it in a project configured for the target platform.
content.why_it_matters: Professional applications need repeatable tests, clear APIs, dependable dependencies, security checks, and observable failures. Apply this concept in small steps before integrating it into a larger project.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: Start with layered architecture. Then compare it with domain, application, and infrastructure responsibilities. Identify the input, state, dependency, or branch that determines the result. The snippet is a static reference for CodeLeaf and is not executed in the lesson page.

items.title: Layered Architecture
items.text: Layered Architecture is one part of architecture and separation of concerns. Connect its definition to the example, identify the input/state it changes, and verify the expected behavior with a small test case.

items.title: Domain, Application, and Infrastructure Responsibilities
items.text: Domain, Application, and Infrastructure Responsibilities should support a clear object invariant: make valid states easy to represent, restrict mutation to the intended API, and keep initialization and dependencies explicit.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in the project that declares the necessary JVM, coroutine, networking, database, or serialization dependencies. Never commit real secrets.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the documented starting values, rerun the smallest test, and compare the result with the expected output. If behavior differs, check the compiler/plugin/runtime versions and the active target before changing more than one thing.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Architecture and Separation of Concerns removes the need to test boundary conditions or verify the chosen runtime/library version.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the example fails, first confirm which runtime/project type the snippet requires. Read the first useful compiler or runtime message, check imports and declared dependencies, reduce the example to a minimal case, and rerun. For target-specific code, use the target toolchain rather than assuming a console or browser runner can execute it.

items.text: Describe the main rule of architecture and separation of concerns in your own words.

items.title: Apply
items.text: Change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

items.title: Verify
items.text: Check one edge case and the official reference for the selected Kotlin/runtime version.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small variation that demonstrates architecture and separation of concerns. Write down your predicted result first, run it in the correct local project, then explain one boundary case involving layered architecture.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain architecture and separation of concerns without copying the lesson wording.
Demonstrate the concept with a small code/configuration change and state the expected result.
Test one boundary case or explain a relevant platform/version limitation.
hints: Begin with the first syllabus subtopic: Layered Architecture. What input or state does it act on?
Change only one value, branch, declaration, or dependency at a time. Predict what should happen before running the code.
Compare your observed result with the expected output and the official reference; verify that you are using the required project type and dependency set.
